subject: Environment
description: Stratospheric vs tropospheric ozone, ODS, Montreal Protocol, Kigali amendment

questions.stem: The ozone layer is mainly located in which layer of the atmosphere?

options.option_text: Troposphere
Stratosphere
Mesosphere
Thermosphere

questions.explanation: The 'good' ozone layer sits in the lower stratosphere — roughly 15-35 km above sea level, with peak concentration ~25 km. It absorbs 97-99% of harmful UV-B radiation. Atmosphere layers (bottom up) — Troposphere (0-12 km), Stratosphere (12-50 km, contains ozone layer), Mesosphere (50-85 km), Thermosphere (85-600 km), Exosphere. Tropospheric ozone (near ground) — different role: a pollutant and greenhouse gas.
questions.subject: Environment

options.option_text: Diatomic molecule
Triatomic allotrope of oxygen
Compound of oxygen and nitrogen
Noble gas

questions.explanation: Ozone (O₃) — three oxygen atoms; an allotropic form of oxygen alongside O₂ (the air we breathe). Bluish, pungent gas. Formed in stratosphere by UV splitting O₂ → 2O, then O + O₂ → O₃ (Chapman cycle, 1930). Half-life depends on temperature/pressure but in stratosphere remains balanced naturally. Major absorber of UV-B (280-315 nm), preventing skin cancer / cataracts / DNA damage on Earth's surface.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The international treaty for phasing out ozone-depleting substances is the:

options.option_text: Kyoto Protocol, 1997
Montreal Protocol, 1987
Paris Agreement, 2015
Stockholm Convention, 2001

questions.explanation: Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer — signed 16 September 1987 (a date now observed as World Ozone Day), came into force 1 Jan 1989. Universally ratified — 198 parties. Phases out CFCs, HCFCs, halons, methyl bromide. Considered the most successful environmental treaty — ozone hole healing observed; full recovery projected by 2066 (Antarctic). Kyoto/Paris target greenhouse gases; Stockholm targets persistent organic pollutants.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The 2016 Kigali Amendment to the Montreal Protocol added phase-down obligations for:

options.option_text: CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons)
HFCs (hydrofluorocarbons)
Methane
Nitrous oxide

questions.explanation: Kigali Amendment (15 Oct 2016, in force 1 Jan 2019) — adds HFCs to the list. HFCs replaced CFCs/HCFCs as refrigerants but turned out to be potent greenhouse gases (1000s× more warming than CO₂). India ratified in Sep 2021. India's HFC schedule: freeze 2028, 10% reduction by 2032, 80% reduction by 2047. Could prevent ~0.5 °C of additional warming by 2100.
questions.subject: Environment

options.option_text: Beneficial gas that protects from UV
Secondary pollutant + greenhouse gas formed from NOx + VOCs in sunlight
Refrigerant
Component of CNG

questions.explanation: Tropospheric ozone — 'bad' ozone — formed when nitrogen oxides (vehicle/industrial exhaust) and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight (photochemical smog, peaks on hot afternoons). Causes lung damage, asthma flare-ups, crop yield loss. Also a short-lived greenhouse gas (3rd biggest after CO₂ and CH₄ globally). Stratospheric ozone protects life; tropospheric ozone harms it. Same molecule, different altitude → opposite role.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: The 'ozone hole' is most pronounced over which region of Earth?

options.option_text: The Arctic, year-round
Antarctica, during the southern spring (Sep-Nov)
Equatorial belt, summer
Indian Ocean, monsoon season

questions.explanation: First reported by British Antarctic Survey scientists Farman, Gardiner, Shanklin in Nature, 1985. The hole appears each austral spring (Sep-Nov) over Antarctica because polar stratospheric clouds (forming below −78 °C in winter) provide surfaces for chlorine activation; sunlight returning in spring then triggers ozone destruction. Largest extent recorded — 2000 (~30 million km²). Recovery underway; Antarctic ozone projected to return to 1980 levels by ~2066.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: Ozone column thickness is measured in:

options.option_text: ppm (parts per million)
Dobson Units (DU)
Watts per m²
Kelvin

questions.explanation: Dobson Unit (DU) — named after British meteorologist G.M.B. Dobson (1920s). 1 DU = ozone column 0.01 mm thick at standard temperature/pressure. Global average ~300 DU; values below 220 DU define the 'ozone hole'. Lowest readings — Antarctica in spring, ~100 DU. Measurement instruments — Dobson spectrophotometer; satellite — TOMS, OMI on Aura satellite. India contributes via Maitri / Bharati Antarctic stations.
questions.subject: Environment

questions.stem: Which chemical species acts as the primary catalytic agent in the destruction of stratospheric ozone, particularly over polar regions?

options.option_text: Chlorine free radicals released by CFC photolysis
Carbon dioxide molecules emitted by burning fossil fuels
Sulfur dioxide aerosols released during volcanic eruptions
Nitrogen dioxide produced in high-temperature combustion

questions.explanation: A is correct because CFCs, once they drift into the stratosphere, are broken down by UV radiation to release chlorine free radicals. One Cl radical can destroy up to 100,000 ozone molecules catalytically. CO₂ (Option B) warms the troposphere but does not react with ozone. SO₂ (Option C) forms aerosols that can modestly affect ozone but is not the primary catalyst. NO₂ (Option D) plays a secondary role via NOₓ cycles but is far less potent than chlorine radicals from CFCs.

questions.stem: The Vienna Convention (1985) and the Montreal Protocol (1987) are closely related international instruments. What was the specific legal purpose of the Vienna Convention?

options.option_text: It created the Multilateral Fund to support developing nations' compliance
It established binding phase-out schedules for all major ODS categories
It served as the framework convention for global ozone layer protection
It immediately banned the production of chlorofluorocarbons worldwide

questions.explanation: C is correct: Vienna Convention is a framework convention — it set general obligations for research and cooperation but contained no specific phase-out schedules. Those binding obligations came two years later with the Montreal Protocol (1987). The Multilateral Fund (Option A) was created by the 1990 London Amendment, not Vienna. Options B and D describe actions of the Montreal Protocol, not the Vienna Convention.

questions.stem: Ozone layer depletion is most directly linked to increased human exposure to which radiation band, driving higher rates of skin cancer, cataracts, and immune suppression?

options.option_text: UV-A (315–400 nm), which largely passes through the ozone layer unhindered
UV-B (280–315 nm), selectively absorbed by stratospheric ozone molecules
UV-C (100–280 nm), which is completely absorbed by both ozone and oxygen
Infrared radiation (700 nm–1 mm), absorbed mainly by water vapour

questions.explanation: B is correct: UV-B (280–315 nm) is the biologically damaging band that ozone absorbs most selectively; even a 1% drop in ozone increases UV-B reaching Earth's surface by about 2%. UV-A (Option A) largely bypasses the ozone layer regardless. UV-C (Option C) is the most energetic but is completely absorbed by stratospheric ozone and molecular oxygen before reaching the surface — its ground-level risk is already near zero even with ozone depletion. Infrared (Option D) has nothing to do with ozone chemistry.

questions.stem: The Ozone Depleting Potential (ODP) scale was established to compare the harmful impact of various substances. Which compound is assigned the reference value of ODP = 1.0?

options.option_text: CFC-12 (dichlorodifluoromethane), once common in refrigeration systems
Halon-1301 (bromotrifluoromethane), deployed as a fire suppressant agent
HCFC-22 (chlorodifluoromethane), used as a transitional refrigerant gas
CFC-11 (trichlorofluoromethane), the internationally accepted ODP benchmark

questions.explanation: D is correct: CFC-11 (CCl₃F) is the reference substance with ODP = 1.0 by international convention. CFC-12 (Option A) has an ODP of approximately 0.82. Halon-1301 (Option B) is actually more destructive with an ODP of about 10 — a common trap since students assume the reference is the most harmful substance. HCFC-22 (Option C) has a much lower ODP of ~0.055, as it breaks down more readily in the troposphere before reaching the stratosphere.

questions.stem: The existence of the Antarctic 'ozone hole' was first formally reported in a landmark 1985 paper published in the journal Nature. Which organisation's researchers made this discovery?

options.option_text: NASA Goddard Institute for Space Studies, headquartered in New York, USA
NOAA's Climate Monitoring and Diagnostics Laboratory based in Boulder
World Meteorological Organisation's Geneva-based ozone monitoring division
British Antarctic Survey scientists Farman, Gardiner, and Shanklin (UK)

questions.explanation: D is correct: Joseph Farman, Brian Gardiner, and Jonathan Shanklin of the British Antarctic Survey published the seminal 1985 Nature paper documenting dramatic springtime ozone depletion over Halley Bay, Antarctica. NASA (Option A) had satellite data but the algorithm had discarded abnormally low readings as instrument error — they confirmed the discovery after the BAS paper, not before. WMO (Option C) and NOAA (Option B) contributed monitoring data but were not the authors of the discovery paper.

questions.stem: Polar Stratospheric Clouds (PSCs) are known to dramatically amplify ozone depletion during polar winter. What is their precise chemical role in this process?

options.option_text: They reflect incoming UV-B back to space, accelerating ozone photodissociation
They trap active chlorine into stable reservoir compounds, temporarily halting loss
They release ozone directly into the troposphere through gravity-wave mixing
Their surfaces host heterogeneous reactions converting chlorine reservoirs to active radicals

questions.explanation: D is correct: PSCs (mainly nitric acid trihydrate and ice crystals) provide solid/liquid surfaces for heterogeneous reactions that convert stable 'reservoir' species — HCl and ClONO₂ — into reactive Cl₂ and HOCl. When polar spring sunlight returns, these photolyze instantly to chlorine radicals that destroy ozone catalytically. Option B describes the exact opposite: PSCs activate, not trap, chlorine. Option A misunderstands the mechanism — PSCs do not reflect UV. Option C conflates PSC chemistry with gravity-wave dynamics, which is a separate phenomenon.

questions.stem: The Antarctic ozone hole is consistently far more severe than any Arctic ozone depletion observed to date. Which scientific factor most fundamentally explains this asymmetry?

options.option_text: CFC concentrations accumulate preferentially over the Antarctic landmass
Antarctica's polar vortex is more stable and isolated, sustaining colder stratospheric air
Antarctica receives significantly less total annual solar radiation than the Arctic
The Arctic stratosphere contains more nitrogen oxides that neutralise chlorine

questions.explanation: B is correct: The Antarctic polar vortex is exceptionally strong and geographically isolated (surrounded by ocean, no major mountain ranges to disrupt flow), keeping stratospheric temperatures below –78°C for months — cold enough for PSCs to form and persist. The Arctic vortex is frequently disrupted by planetary waves from Eurasia's mountain chains, warming the stratosphere and limiting PSC formation. CFCs (Option A) are uniformly distributed globally, not concentrated over Antarctica. Total solar radiation (Option C) is roughly comparable; the key is stratospheric temperature, not solar intensity. While NOₓ (Option D) can deactivate chlorine somewhat, this is a minor secondary effect and does not explain the primary asymmetry.
